sections.text:
Ephesians looks at God’s purpose on the widest scale: to bring everything together under Christ. The first three chapters praise God for choosing, forgiving and raising believers with Christ, by grace and through faith, and for making Jews and non-Jews into one new people.

The last three chapters describe a life that fits this calling: unity, truthful speech, forgiveness, relationships in the household, and standing firm in what the letter pictures as the armor of God.

The letter presents itself as written by Paul from prison. The words in Ephesus are missing from some of the earliest copies, so it may have been a circular letter for several churches. Some scholars think a follower of Paul wrote it in his name.

The instructions to wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters (5:21 to 6:9) are read in different ways. Some see a lasting pattern for marriage; others stress the opening call to submit to one another and see the passage pointing toward mutuality. The words to slaves were misused to defend slavery, a reading churches now reject.
